title: Your simran, chosen
hook: decide when you'll remember each day
tomorrow: at dawn the Granth opens to a page. what will it say to her?

segments.voice: What a week. The long story, ending on the good of all. The ways, with one light under them. Then the choosing: a Nitnem on a sticky note, seva where the hands go, a sangat named out loud, and yesterday's line, my share, on a napkin.
screen: `THE LONG STORY.` → `THE WAYS.` → `MY NITNEM.` → `MY SEVA.` → `MY SANGAT.` → `MY SHARE.`

segments.voice: Simran's fall schedule is finally in her calendar app: classes in blue, the pantry in green, Sundays at the student gurdwara group in orange. Four things chosen. The fifth one on her list has no color yet, and it's the one she was named for. Simran. She scrolls the week looking for an empty hour and can't find one. Bebe, reading over her shoulder, laughs. That one doesn't need an hour, she says.
screen: `FOUR THINGS IN COLOR.` → `THE FIFTH HAS NO SLOT.` → `IT DOESN'T NEED AN HOUR.`

segments.voice: Simran, the practice, is remembering the Name, often Waheguru, said on a breath or a bead. Bebe gives her two places to put it. The first is old: the Japji's fourth pauri praises the ambrosial hours before dawn, amrit vela, as the time to reflect on the true Name. A few minutes before the dorm wakes up would do. The second fits a full calendar. Kabir has a salok on Ang 1376, paraphrased: do all your work with your hands and feet, and keep your mind with the Pure One. So the Name goes on the walk between classes, at the sink, on the bus. Simran remembers the mala from Bebe that sat in her drawer all year, the one she finally used while she waited on that school email. It goes in her bag. In the calendar, she adds one line at the top of every day, no color at all: Waheguru.
screen: `REMEMBERING THE NAME.` · `AMRIT VELA, BEFORE DAWN.` · `HANDS AT WORK, MIND WITH THE ONE.` · `THE MALA GOES IN THE BAG.` · then, large: `MY SIMRAN.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and say Waheguru silently on each breath out, or any word that steadies you. Near the end of the sit, ask when it will fit tomorrow: before the day starts, on a walk, at the sink. Pick one, and keep it.
Your simran: when you choose to remember the Name each day, at dawn, at work, or both.
Keep this one: my simran, at dawn and between the doing. Five chosen, and one more week on the summit.

screen: `DAY 1778 COUNTS.` → `THE SUMMIT · 18 OF 31.` → `TOMORROW: THE GRANTH OPENS AT DAWN. WHAT DOES IT SAY?`

howItsDone: Sikhs practice simran by repeating the Name, often Waheguru, in the early hours of amrit vela, during kirtan, with a mala, or silently while working, walking and traveling.

fork.setup: a friend who works double shifts as a nurse says she has no time left to remember God. what does this week's teaching offer her?
options: the Name can go with her hands at work, and a breath of it before sleep.
she should drop a shift, since real remembering only happens at dawn.
her work already counts as prayer, so she doesn't need to remember at all.
fork.reveal: Kabir puts it plainly: hands at work, mind with the One. amrit vela is a gift when it's there; simran fits between the doing too.

original.note: Gurmukhi: remembering the Name, and the friend's own name.

trapdoor: what you thought: simran is a long meditation session you need a free hour for.
what it means: remembering the Name, at dawn and in the middle of work, at a time you choose and keep.

chat.says: nitnem, seva, sangat, daswandh: done. my calendar is full. where does simran even fit?
options: a few minutes at amrit vela, then the Name on the walk between classes.
only before dawn; simran at any other time of day doesn't count.
wait until a free hour opens up; simran needs quiet and nothing else.
chat.meaning: The Japji praises the hours before dawn, and Kabir says keep the mind with the One while the hands work. Simran fits both.

Waheguru.meaning: a Sikh name for the One, often repeated in simran

mala.meaning: a string of beads moved one at a time with the Name

Kabir.meaning: a weaver-poet whose hymns are in the Granth

Japji.meaning: Guru Nanak's hymn that opens the Guru Granth Sahib
